questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Identify the keystone species in a designed habitat
questions.stem: An architect plans a coastal boardwalk whose paving hides a large population of the shore crab that keeps mussels from crowding out kelp.

options.text: The crab is a keystone species, because it holds more biomass than the mussels it eats
options.misconception: defines keystone status by biomass rather than effect

options.text: The crab is a producer, because the kelp beds depend on the light it lets through
options.misconception: treats a predator as the source of primary production

options.text: The crab is a foundation species, because the paving stones rest on its burrows
options.misconception: confuses a habitat builder with a keystone predator

options.text: The crab is a keystone species, because its presence holds the kelp community together

questions.explanation: A keystone species has a community effect large relative to its own abundance, and the crab sets the balance between mussels and kelp. Removing it would let mussels dominate the shore.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to the community if the crab goes.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Calculate how many individuals a plot can support for a species
questions.stem: A courtyard brief allocates 500 square metres of planting, and two competing ground-nesting bird species each need a minimum of 25 square metres. How many birds of that species can the plot support?
questions.explanation: With 500 square metres available and 25 needed per bird, the plot supports 500 divided by 25, which is 20 birds. With two species needing that space, all 20 are contested.
questions.hint: Divide the total area by the area needed per bird.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a claim that predator numbers cause prey crashes
questions.stem: A park manager proposes widening footpaths so that visitors keep the vole population low enough to protect the flower beds.

options.text: Disturbance is unlikely to act like a predator, since it removes no animals from the population
options.misconception: assumes only predation can reduce a prey population

options.text: Disturbance will make the vole population cycle, exactly as a fox population would
options.misconception: claims a non-predatory pressure makes the same cycle

options.text: Disturbance can hold prey numbers down, but it is a different kind of control from predation
Disturbance will do nothing, because predator numbers set the size of every prey population
options.misconception: claims predators are the only control on a prey population

questions.explanation: Footpath pressure can cut vole survival and so control numbers, but it does not produce the linked rise and fall of a predator-prey cycle, in which each species limits the other.
questions.hint: Ask whether the two populations limit each other.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Interpret survey data showing different niche use by two species
questions.stem: A garden survey finds species A feeding on seven microhabitats and species B on three, with two of the habitats shared.

options.text: Species A is a generalist, so species B must be excluded from the garden entirely
options.misconception: assumes a wider niche always removes the other species

options.text: Species A occupies the wider niche and takes more of the resources on offer
Species B holds the wider niche, because sharing habitats is a sign of specialisation
options.misconception: reads a narrow feeding record as a broad niche

options.text: Both species hold the same niche, since the two shared habitats are the only ones that count
options.misconception: equates niche breadth with the number of shared habitats

questions.explanation: A niche covers the range of resources and conditions a species uses, and species A takes seven garden microhabitats against three for species B. The two shared habitats show partial overlap.
questions.hint: Count the habitats each species actually uses.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Identify an abiotic factor that limits a designed planting
questions.stem: An architect's planting plan for a rooftop meadow fails every summer because the surface bakes and the soil dries out completely.

options.text: Heat and moisture are biotic factors, because they act on living plant tissue directly
options.misconception: classifies physical conditions as living components

options.text: The rooftop has too many species, so the abiotic problem is caused by planting variety
options.misconception: blames a physical limit on the number of species planted

options.text: The plants were planted in the wrong season, so the summer heat is really a planting date issue
options.misconception: reduces a physical limit to a scheduling mistake

options.text: Heat and moisture are abiotic factors, since they are physical conditions rather than living organisms

questions.explanation: Abiotic limiting factors are the non-living conditions of a habitat, such as temperature, water, light and wind, that set what can live there. On an exposed roof, heat and moisture set the ceiling.
questions.hint: Ask whether the factor is alive or a physical condition.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the per capita rate of increase for a population
questions.stem: A garden survey of a vole colony counts 200 animals, with 140 young produced and 40 deaths recorded over one breeding season. What is the per capita rate of increase for the colony?
questions.explanation: The per capita rate of increase is the number added divided by the starting population, so 100 divided by 200 gives 0.5. Such a high value marks an r selected species with large broods.
questions.hint: Divide the net gain by the starting population.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a population can overshoot its carrying capacity
questions.stem: A visitor centre pond that was stocked with fish now has too many fish and the water is turning to sludge.

options.text: The pond's carrying capacity has fallen, so the same fish are now too many for it
options.misconception: blames a falling capacity for a stocking error

options.text: The fish overshot the pond's capacity, and waste from the excess stock is now the problem
The pond cannot have a carrying capacity, because only wild ponds count as habitats
options.misconception: denies that built ponds have a limiting capacity

options.text: The pond is fine, because a stocking level can never exceed what the water supports
options.misconception: assumes stocking always lands at or below capacity

questions.explanation: A population can grow past the point a habitat supports, and the excess then weakens the system through waste, oxygen loss and disease, which is why this pond has both too many fish and poor water.
questions.hint: Consider the order of stocking and fouling.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Compare two populations growing at different rates
questions.stem: A landscape plan compares two grass species, one spreading at 10 percent a year and one at 20 percent a year from equal starting covers.

options.text: The faster species always stays ahead by exactly the same margin each year
options.misconception: assumes a constant absolute gap between the two species

options.text: Both species will settle at the same size, because the plot has a fixed total area
options.misconception: assumes a fixed area forces identical final covers

options.text: The faster species will overtake the slower one, since the gap widens as the years pass
The slower species will win, because slower growth protects a species from being outcompeted
options.misconception: reverses the link between growth rate and success

questions.explanation: When two species start equal and one multiplies faster, the gap grows each year rather than staying constant, so the faster species takes a larger share of the plot.
questions.hint: Compare the two covers year by year.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain when a biomass pyramid can turn upside down
questions.stem: A design brief for a canal-side pond notes that the fish biomass exceeds the plankton biomass beneath them.

options.text: An inverted pyramid is impossible, because a pyramid always narrows toward the top
options.misconception: assumes biomass pyramids always narrow upward

options.text: An inverted pyramid is impossible, because the fish are visibly bigger than the plankton
options.misconception: argues from individual body size to pyramid shape

options.text: An inverted pyramid is possible, because the plankton are replaced faster than the fish eat them
An inverted pyramid is likely, because all aquatic systems work this way
options.misconception: generalises one exceptional pattern to every aquatic system

questions.explanation: Standing biomass depends on how fast a level is renewed, and a small crop of plankton can support a heavier crop of fish when turnover is fast, so a biomass pyramid can widen upward in a pond.
questions.hint: Consider how quickly the plankton population is replaced.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the resource total when units are shared between two species
questions.stem: A habitat brief describes two species needing 5 and 4 resource units, where 2 units are shared between them. How many resource units are actually required once the shared units are counted only once?
questions.explanation: Without sharing the two species would need 5 plus 4, which is 9 units, but the 2 shared units are used once, so only 7 are needed. Partitioning like this lets both species coexist with less resource.
questions.hint: Add the two needs, then subtract the shared units once.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Judge whether a species is a keystone in a proposed design
questions.stem: A brief proposes removing the sea otter population from a rocky shore design to protect the mussel beds for visitors.

options.text: Removing the otter is wise, because otters damage the mussels more than the kelp benefits
options.misconception: judges the keystone role only by the effect on one species

options.text: Removing the otter is wise, because kelp forests are the least valuable part of the shore
options.misconception: ranks a habitat by appearance rather than ecological role

options.text: Removing the otter makes no difference, because the shore will settle to the same balance anyway
options.misconception: assumes a keystone species has no community effect

options.text: Removing the otter is unwise, because the mussels would then crowd out the kelp and change the whole shore

questions.explanation: The otter is a keystone predator because it holds the mussel population in check, and without it mussels take the space and the kelp is lost. The brief should keep the otter habitat instead.
questions.hint: Trace the effect of losing the predator.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Interpret data showing one species excluding another
questions.stem: A wetland plot survey records plant species A at 400 plants per square metre and species B at 5, with both using the same root depth.

options.text: Species B is simply rarer, because abundance always reflects the size of a species population
options.misconception: treats low abundance as rarity rather than competition

options.text: Species B is being excluded, because the two species compete for the same rooting depth
Species A must be a better coloniser, because the two species occupy identical root depths
options.misconception: reads shared rooting depth as evidence of colonisation

options.text: Neither species is affected, since plants of different heights never compete for root space
options.misconception: assumes competition only happens between similar species

questions.explanation: Two species using exactly the same limited resource cannot coexist indefinitely, and the one better at using it drives the other out. The very low count of species B fits exclusion.
questions.hint: Ask what both species are taking from the same pool.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Describe the lagged relationship in a predator-prey cycle
questions.stem: A brief for a bird hide describes hare numbers rising and falling while the foxes that hunt them follow behind.

options.text: Fox numbers rise before hares, because foxes always breed ahead of their prey
options.misconception: reverses the order of the two populations in the cycle

options.text: Hares and foxes rise together, because both simply follow the spring plant growth
options.misconception: reduces a predator-prey cycle to a shared seasonal driver

options.text: Fox numbers rise after hares, because abundant hares feed a larger fox population
Hare numbers stay level, because foxes prevent them from ever increasing
options.misconception: assumes predation holds the prey flat at all times

questions.explanation: Predator numbers lag behind their prey, because abundant prey supports a larger predator population, which then cuts the prey back. The two curves therefore rise and fall in sequence.
questions.hint: Ask which population increases first.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Calculate how many habitats a pair of species occupies together
questions.stem: A reserve has five microhabitats. Species A uses three of them, species B uses three, and they share exactly one. How many microhabitats are used by at least one of the two species?
questions.explanation: Adding the two records of use gives 3 plus 3, which is 6, but the one shared habitat was counted twice, so 6 minus 1 leaves 5 habitats occupied, matching the five the reserve offers.
questions.hint: Add the two totals, then subtract the shared habitat once.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Reason about which physical factor a design must control
questions.stem: A quarry reclamation brief says the site will only succeed if the wall shades the whole south face for the first two summers.

options.text: The concern is misplaced, because shade affects only plants and no other factor matters
options.misconception: assumes one abiotic factor is always the only one

options.text: The concern is misplaced, because heat and shade are regulated by the plants themselves
options.misconception: assumes plants control their own physical environment

options.text: The brief is right, because soil depth is never limiting on a reclaimed site
options.misconception: treats one physical factor as irrelevant in all settings

options.text: Shade and heat are both abiotic, and water availability will matter at least as much on a bare quarry

questions.explanation: Shade and temperature are abiotic conditions, and on bare reclaimed ground the water supply usually matters as much, so a brief built on one physical factor alone will leave planting short of water.
questions.hint: Consider what a bare surface loses fastest in summer.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Interpret survey data that separate r and K selected species
questions.stem: A garden survey records species A producing 200 young each year with a 95 percent juvenile survival rate, while species B produces 6 young that live for 15 years.

options.text: Species A is K selected, because a high survival rate always marks a stable population
options.misconception: reads high juvenile survival as a sign of K selection

options.text: Species A is r selected and species B is K selected, given their very different life histories
Both species are K selected, because the garden is a stable and protected habitat
options.misconception: judges life history by the habitat rather than the species

options.text: Species B is r selected, because long-lived species always reproduce more quickly
options.misconception: confuses lifespan with reproductive rate

questions.explanation: Species A produces many young with high early survival, the r selected pattern, while species B produces few young and invests in long life, the K selected pattern.
questions.hint: Compare young produced and lifespan for each species.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Predict the outcome of a population that has overshot capacity
questions.stem: A meadow restoration has a rabbit population of 900 in a habitat that can carry only 600 animals.

options.text: Numbers will rise further, because a larger population always supports faster growth
options.misconception: assumes more individuals always means a faster increase

options.text: Numbers will fall, because overcrowding will raise disease and starvation among the rabbits
Numbers will stay at 900, because the grass grew well during the wet spring
options.misconception: treats one good season as a permanent raise in capacity

options.text: Numbers will double, because the predators have not yet responded to the increase
options.misconception: assumes predator response adds to growth

questions.explanation: Above carrying capacity the resources per animal are too low, so disease, starvation and predation cut the numbers back down, and the crash after an overshoot returns the population to capacity.
questions.hint: Consider what happens when demand exceeds grass growth.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the gap between two differently growing populations
questions.stem: A dredging plan compares two plant populations of 500 each, one growing 40 percent a year and the other 20 percent a year. What is the difference between the two populations after one year?
questions.explanation: After one year the faster population reaches 500 times 1.4, which is 700, and the slower reaches 500 times 1.2, which is 600, so the gap is 100 individuals.
questions.hint: Grow each population by its rate, then subtract.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish an energy pyramid from a biomass pyramid
questions.stem: A boardwalk brief shows an energy pyramid that narrows upward and a biomass pyramid for the same pond that widens.

options.text: One of them must be wrong, because a single habitat can only have one pyramid
options.misconception: assumes a habitat supports only one type of pyramid

options.text: The energy pyramid is wrong, because energy is always conserved between trophic levels
options.misconception: treats energy conservation as biomass conservation

options.text: Both are correct, because energy is lost upward while standing biomass depends on turnover rate
The biomass pyramid is wrong, because biomass always follows energy upward level by level
options.misconception: assumes standing biomass must track the energy at each level

questions.explanation: Energy always falls as it moves upward, so the energy pyramid narrows, while standing biomass depends on how fast each level is renewed and can be wider at the top in a productive pond.
questions.hint: Ask whether the two measures depend on turnover.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Interpret survey data showing resource partitioning
questions.stem: A survey finds two pond species eating different parts of the same weed bed, with each taking only a small share of it.

options.text: The species coexist because the weed bed is unlimited, so nothing competes for it
options.misconception: explains coexistence by assuming an unlimited resource

options.text: The species coexist because they occupy different habitats, so they never meet at all
options.misconception: confuses sharing a habitat with occupying separate ones

options.text: The species coexist because the predator keeps both of them at low numbers
options.misconception: credits a predator for what resource partitioning achieves

options.text: The species coexist by partitioning the resource, so neither has to fight for all of it

questions.explanation: Partitioning the weed bed into different parts lowers the overlap between the two species, so each can persist in the same habitat. Coexistence like this comes from reduced competition.
questions.hint: Ask whether the two species take the same parts of the food.

options.text: The sea stars are a keystone species, because they hold the mussel population in check
The sea stars are a keystone species, because they are the only species with a hard shell

options.text: The sea stars are a keystone species, because removing them would let the rock become bare
options.misconception: predicts the opposite of the real community effect

questions.explanation: A keystone species has a disproportionately large effect on community structure, and the sea stars control the mussels that would otherwise dominate the shore.

questions.explanation: Eighty percent of the 200 resource units is 160 units, and those are the ones both species compete over, and overlap of this kind is the condition under which exclusion can drive one species out.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how a predator can help its prey population
questions.stem: A grazing brief says that removing wolves from a valley will cause the deer population to fall within a few years.

options.misconception: invents a reproductive cost of predation

options.text: The claim is right, because wolves keep the grass so short that deer cannot find enough to eat
options.misconception: gives the predator a purely beneficial effect on its prey

options.text: The claim is backwards, because without wolves the deer grow until the pasture fails and the herd crashes
The claim is right, because without wolves the deer lose their sense of direction and wander off
options.misconception: credits predator removal with a heritable behaviour change

questions.learningObjective: Explain how a species broadens its niche when a competitor arrives
questions.stem: A survey finds the pond species using the same weed bed as before, but also feeding on algae that it previously ignored.

options.text: The species has narrowed its niche, because adding a food source reduces its options
options.misconception: treats a wider diet as a narrower niche

options.text: The species has changed its habitat, so it must now live somewhere different
options.misconception: confuses a change in diet with a change of habitat

options.text: The species has not changed at all, because a niche is fixed for the whole of a species lifetime
options.misconception: assumes a niche can never shift within a lifetime

options.text: The species has broadened its niche, so it now competes with more neighbours for food

questions.explanation: A niche is the range of resources a species actually uses, and taking algae as well as the weed bed widens that range, which is one route by which competition pushes a species elsewhere.

questions.stem: A brief describes a clear water tank where a small mass of algae supports a large mass of zooplankton.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Read competitive exclusion from a survey record
questions.stem: A pond survey finds three snail species, but one accounts for 95 percent of the individuals and the other two only appear where the first is absent.

options.text: The two rare species persist because the dominant species creates better habitat for them
options.misconception: turns a competition outcome into a facilitation effect

options.text: The two rare species persist because they are simply at the very start of their spread
options.misconception: explains low numbers as a stage in a range expansion

options.text: The two rare species are not really present, because the survey only counted the dominant one
options.misconception: treats recorded individuals as a counting error

options.text: The two rare species persist by using resources the dominant species does not

questions.explanation: Where the dominant species is absent the two rare species use resources it does not, so they are limited by competition rather than conditions, and that partitioning is what lets them persist.
questions.hint: Notice where the rare species are found.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a shared predator can link two prey species
questions.stem: A brief asks why the disappearance of one bird species led to a sharp rise in the number of snails it shared a predator with.

options.text: The snails and the bird competed for the same food, so removing the bird released the snails
options.misconception: describes a competitor link as a shared predator effect

options.text: The two prey species compete for the same predator, so freeing one let that predator grow on the other
The snails and the bird had a mutual relationship, so removing the bird freed the snails
options.misconception: calls a predator link a mutual benefit

options.text: The snails and the bird filled the same niche, so removing the bird left the niche empty
options.misconception: treats the shared predator as a shared niche

questions.explanation: Two prey species that feed the same predator compete indirectly, and the predator numbers set how much predation each gets, so removing one prey species lets the predator grow and push down the other.
questions.hint: Consider what happens to the shared predator's numbers.

questions.stem: A habitat offers six microhabitats, and a survey shows one species occupying four of them. How many microhabitats are left for other species?
questions.explanation: With six microhabitats available and four occupied, the number left for other species is 6 minus 4, which is 2, and those two habitats are the space a second species could use.

questions.learningObjective: Reason about how a physical factor restricts a community
questions.stem: A coastal brief records that a salt marsh supports far fewer plant species than the field beside it.

options.text: The marsh has fewer predators, so it must be easier for plants to establish there
options.misconception: uses predator numbers to explain plant diversity

options.text: The two habitats share the same plants, so the marsh count must be a survey error
options.misconception: assumes identical species lists across very different soils

options.text: Salinity and waterlogging are abiotic factors, and they restrict which plants can grow there
The marsh is simply older, so it has had more time to lose its plant species
options.misconception: invents a time explanation for a physical constraint

questions.explanation: The salt content and waterlogged soil of a marsh are abiotic conditions that only a narrow set of plants can tolerate, so the number of species that can live there is set from the start.
questions.hint: Ask what the salt and the water table do to plant growth.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Compare life histories typical of r and K selected species
questions.stem: A survey compares a weed that makes 2,000 seeds with a slow-growing tree that makes 40 seeds and lives for 200 years.

options.text: The weed is K selected, because a high seed count guarantees a long-lived population
options.misconception: treats high fecundity as evidence of long life

options.text: The tree is r selected, because it lives longer than the weed
options.misconception: reads lifespan as a sign of rapid reproduction

options.text: Both are K selected, because they both live in the same designed habitat
options.misconception: judges life history by the habitat rather than by the traits

options.text: The weed is r selected and the tree is K selected, given their contrasting life histories

questions.explanation: Thousands of seeds with no investment in individual survival is the r selected pattern, while a few seeds and a very long life is the K selected pattern. The life history decides it, not the habitat.
questions.hint: Compare seed number with lifespan for the two species.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish an overshoot from a steady approach to capacity
questions.stem: A meadow brief describes a rabbit population that peaked at 900, crashed to 400, and has since crept back to 500.

options.text: This is a steady approach, because the final level is the same as the capacity
options.misconception: equates the end point with the whole pattern of change

options.text: This is an overshoot, in which the population passed capacity and then crashed back
This is a predator cycle, because a rising population is always followed by a falling one
options.misconception: attributes an overshoot to a predator-prey cycle

options.text: This is a growth failure, because a population that overshoots has failed to reproduce
options.misconception: reads a population crash as a reproductive failure

questions.explanation: An overshoot is defined by the population passing its carrying capacity before falling back, usually because growth runs ahead of the resource response.
questions.hint: Look at where the peak sits relative to the capacity.

questions.explanation: After two years the faster population reaches 2,000 times 1.1 squared, which is 2,420, and the slower reaches 2,000 times 1.05 squared, which is 2,205, so the gap is 215 individuals.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Compare energy and biomass measures in a designed water feature
questions.stem: A brief for a water feature notes that energy falls upward from algae to zooplankton to fish, while standing biomass rises.

options.text: Only the biomass figure is right, because energy in a food web never changes between levels
options.misconception: denies the losses that drive the energy pyramid

options.text: Only the energy figure is right, because standing biomass always follows the energy pattern
options.misconception: assumes the two measures must move together

options.text: Both are correct, because biomass measures standing stock and energy measures the flow through each level
Neither is right, because a food web cannot be described by pyramids at all
options.misconception: denies that a web can be summarised as a pyramid

questions.explanation: Energy is a flow and biomass is a stock, so a level with fast turnover can hold a small standing biomass while passing much energy upward, and the two measures can look opposite.
questions.hint: Ask whether the measure is a flow or a standing amount.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how resource partitioning allows two species to persist
questions.stem: A brief says that a newly arrived species will certainly displace the resident herbivores because it feeds on the same plants.

options.text: The claim is correct, because any overlap at all guarantees exclusion of the resident species
options.misconception: treats partial overlap as certain exclusion

options.text: The claim is correct, because the resident species have no defence against a new competitor
options.misconception: assumes a resident species has no competitive edge

options.text: The claim is too certain, because the resident species will simply leave the habitat voluntarily
options.misconception: invents voluntary departure as a response to competition

options.text: The claim is too certain, because the newcomer may use the plants at a different time or height

questions.explanation: Species often coexist because they take the same resource in different ways, by feeding at a different height, in a different season or on a different part of the plant.

questions.stem: A forest brief records that beavers fell the trees that create the ponds in which many other species then breed.

options.misconception: defines keystone status by numbers rather than effect

options.text: The beaver is a keystone species, because its activity creates habitat for a whole community
The beaver is a keystone species, because the forest cannot regenerate without it
options.misconception: overstates the effect as complete dependence of the habitat

options.text: The beaver is a foundation species, because the trees it fells are the base of the food web
options.misconception: confuses a habitat modifier with a producer

questions.explanation: A keystone species has an effect on community structure far greater than its abundance suggests, and the beaver dams create the ponds many species need, so losing it would lose that community.
questions.hint: Ask what the community would lose if it went.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Predict a management outcome from a predator-prey relationship
questions.stem: A brief proposes adding foxes to a valley to bring the hare numbers down.

options.text: Adding foxes will work permanently, because predator numbers stay at the level they are released at
options.misconception: assumes a released predator population stays fixed forever

options.text: Adding foxes will fail at once, because hares and foxes can never occupy the same valley
options.misconception: assumes predators and prey cannot share a habitat

options.text: Adding foxes may work for a time, but the fox population will also rise and the hares will be hit harder
Adding foxes will fail at once, because foxes eat far more hares than the valley can replace
options.misconception: invents immediate over-predation the numbers do not show

questions.explanation: A predator-prey link produces cycling, so more foxes mean more hares eaten now but a larger fox population later, and the hares then fall below their starting point.

questions.learningObjective: Describe the niche of a species in a designed habitat

options.text: The species occupies a niche defined only by the height at which it feeds
options.misconception: reduces a niche to a single spatial variable

options.text: The species occupies two separate niches, because it feeds on two different plants
options.misconception: counts different food items as separate niches

options.text: The species occupies a niche set entirely by the flowers it prefers
options.misconception: ignores the timing and place that also shape a niche

options.text: The species occupies a niche defined by where, when and on what it feeds

questions.explanation: A niche covers the full range of conditions and resources a species uses, including place, season and food, and the hoverfly use of two heights and two flowering seasons shows how broad that can be.
questions.hint: Include the time and the place, not only the food.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Identify an abiotic factor operating on a marine habitat
questions.stem: A harbour wall design supports only sparse weed, and measurements show the rock surface warms to 30 degrees in summer sun.

options.text: Temperature is limiting, because the exposed rock gets too hot for the weed to survive
Predation is limiting, because exposed rock always shelters more grazers than sheltered rock
options.misconception: invents a predator difference between rock types

options.text: Salinity is limiting, because the harbour wall sits in salt water and the weed is a freshwater plant
options.misconception: assumes marine weed must be a freshwater species

options.text: Nitrogen is limiting, because bare rock cannot hold any of the nutrients from the sea
options.misconception: treats bare rock as unable to hold any nutrient at all

questions.explanation: Temperature is an abiotic factor, and 30 degrees on an exposed surface is enough to stop the weed thriving whatever the nutrient supply, and the measured condition tells the designer what to change.
questions.hint: Ask which measured condition is at an extreme.

questions.stem: A wetland survey counts 250 birds with a per capita rate of increase of 0.4 over one year. How many birds are present after the year?
questions.explanation: The individuals added equal the starting population times the rate of increase, so 250 times 0.4 gives 100 new birds, and adding those to the original 250 gives 350 after the year.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Judge whether a stocking plan risks an overshoot
questions.stem: A brief proposes stocking a pond to its calculated capacity in one single release.

options.text: One large release is risky, because the fish breed before the pond can adjust and may overshoot
One large release is safe, because a pond stocked to capacity can never exceed it
options.misconception: assumes stocking exactly to capacity prevents any overshoot

options.text: One large release is risky, because the fish will ignore the new pond and swim away
options.misconception: invents a dispersal response to stocking

options.text: One large release is safe, because stocking removes any need to monitor the population later
options.misconception: assumes stocking ends the need for management

questions.explanation: Growth continues after the release, so a pond stocked exactly to capacity will move above it as the fish reproduce, and a lower target with staged additions leaves room and avoids the crash.
questions.hint: Consider what the stocked fish do after release.

options.text: The faster species will take over the plot, because the gap between them widens every year
The faster species will take over, because both species must reach the same final size

options.text: The slower species will take over, because slower growth lets a species use the soil more efficiently
options.misconception: invents an efficiency advantage for slow growth

options.text: Neither will take over, because the plot area fixes the final cover for each species
options.misconception: assumes a fixed area forces a fixed outcome

questions.explanation: With equal starting cover the 30 percent species pulls further ahead each year and eventually occupies most of the plot, leaving the slow grower less space.
questions.hint: Track the two covers year by year from an equal start.

options.misconception: generalises one aquatic example to all pools

A rare species cannot be keystone, since keystone species are always common

options.misconception: sets a numeric threshold that defines keystone status
